I have a friend who hates Family Guy. Whenever I hang out with him in a group, or introduce him to other people, he often makes a point to change the topic of conversation to his opinions on that particular Adult Swim cartoon, which can be boiled down to this: Family Guy sucks, and it isn't funny.

In fact, this dialogue comes up so often that I've had plenty of opportunities to voice, and then re-evaluate, my position on the matter. Obviously, the low-hanging fruit argument would be the classic, “well, that just, like, your opinion, man”, but the thing is, he already knows it's his opinion – the problem, it seems, is that he thinks his opinion has more weight behind it than it does. Let me explain.

I could argue that Vincent van Gogh wasn't a good artist. I wouldn't be incorrect, from a factual standpoint, because the word “good” is subjective.

I could argue that Gordon Ramsey makes shitty food. It doesn't matter that he cooks for one of the finest restaurants in the world, a Michelin 3-star establishment, or that his meals have won awards from some of the most respectable food critics alive. If I think his Beef Wellington sucks, then I think it sucks. No one gets to decide that for me.

Except that, while words like “shitty,” “good”, and “funny” are all open to individual interpretation, the general consensus seems to be that Gordon Ramsey is an exceptional chef – and, likewise, Family Guy is a funny show. It scored an 8.3 out of 10 on IMDB, from 220,000 ratings. I could understand not watching it, or perhaps even not liking it, but what I want to figure out is what makes some people feel such a strong desire to be in the vocal minority that opposes it.

If I had to speculate, I'd say it comes down to three possibilities:

First, there is a chance, however small, that my friend actually took the time to sit down and give the sitcom an honest evaluation – watching at least the first couple seasons, and comparing those episodes to some of the later ones, to see how the humor has changed and evolved overtime. I doubt it.

Second, and more likely, is that he's using the show's popularity to supplement his personality. It's no longer interesting to say that you love something when everybody else does, and it's never been interesting to take a middle ground – but hate, that's something to talk about. It invokes a tribal response. It's also a way to make yourself seem more unique without doing anything to earn it. Which, for my friend, is ideal, considering his lack of natural talent. It's the difference between “I ate at Gordon Ramsey's and it was pretty good,” and “I ate at Gordon Ramsey's and it made me wanna barf”. Our opinions are the stories that make up who we are.

The third, and final possibility is that sometimes, in our expectations, we lose sight of what's realistic. We've all been oversold and under-delivered. We're all a little jaded. Still, when the next “big thing” comes around, we somehow manage to, once again, get caught up in the mania – and not until it's over do we look back and think, “that's what all the fuss was about?”. We build our expectations so high that we set ourselves up for disappointment. I suppose this can make use feel deceived, but it doesn't have to. It's okay to look at Starry Night and think it's a little small.

I doubt my friend and I will ever settle our argument, but it's no longer an argument about Family Guy. I encourage whoever is reading this to replace the term “Family Guy” with whatever is popular at the moment, and the output will be, more or less, the same. It's an argument on us as human beings. Our tribal nature. It's an argument on whether or not some opinions are more equal than others.
